nameStory: The Northern Flicker gets its name from the flickering flash of bright yellow or orange you see under its wings and tail when it flies. This sudden burst of color appears to 'flicker' like a candle flame as the bird takes flight, making it unmistakable even from a distance.
description: The Northern Flicker is a medium-sized woodpecker about the size of a robin, but chunkier and more robust. Unlike other woodpeckers that stay glued to tree trunks, flickers spend much of their time hopping around on the ground hunting for ants. They have brownish backs with black bars, spotted breasts, and a distinctive black bib across their upper chest. The most striking feature is the bright yellow or orange color hidden under their wings and tail that flashes dramatically when they fly.

idTips.label: Wing Flash
idTips.description: Brilliant yellow or orange underwings and tail visible only in flight - creates an unmistakable flickering effect that gives this bird its name

idTips.label: Ground Behavior
idTips.description: Hops awkwardly on the ground probing for ants with its slightly curved bill - unusual behavior for a woodpecker

idTips.label: Spotted Breast
idTips.description: Buff-colored chest and belly covered in distinct round black spots, with a prominent black crescent bib across the upper chest

idTips.label: Barred Back
idTips.description: Brown back and wings marked with bold black bars that create a ladder-like pattern when viewed up close

idTips.label: Undulating Flight
idTips.description: Flies in a distinctive up-and-down roller coaster pattern typical of woodpeckers, but the wing flash makes it obvious

idTips.label: Loud Calls
idTips.description: Makes a loud, ringing 'wick-wick-wick' call and a long, descending 'klee-yer' that carries far through the woods

habitat: Northern Flickers thrive in open woodlands, forest edges, parks, and suburban areas with mature trees and open ground for foraging. They prefer areas where woods meet fields or lawns, giving them both nesting sites in dead trees and access to ant colonies in the soil. You'll often spot them in cemeteries, golf courses, and wooded neighborhoods throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity as birds return from migration and begin courtship drumming on metal surfaces like gutters and signs. Males show off their bright wing patches in elaborate displays.
seasonality.summer: Busy feeding young and frequently seen on lawns hunting ants. Adults may appear worn and less colorful by late summer after breeding season.
seasonality.fall: Northern populations begin migrating south, though some remain year-round. Birds may gather in loose flocks and are often seen at bird feeders.
seasonality.winter: Many birds migrate, but hardy individuals remain and visit suet feeders regularly. Winter birds often appear fluffed up and may roost in tree cavities.

funFact: Northern Flickers are one of the few woodpeckers that migrate, with some flying as far as Central America for winter - quite a journey for a bird that spends most of its time hopping around on the ground eating ants!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other woodpeckers when perched, but the wing flash in flight is absolutely diagnostic. On the ground, beginners might mistake them for a thrush or robin due to the spotted breast, but flickers are much larger and hop rather than run.
contextualKnowledge: This species has over 100 folk names including 'yellowhammer,' 'wake-up,' and 'yarrup' - most of these colorful names come from people trying to imitate the bird's varied calls. Don't confuse the American 'yellowhammer' name with the completely different European yellowhammer, which is actually a type of bunting.
compareHints: Northern Flickers are the only flickers in New England, making them unique among local woodpeckers. Compared to other woodpeckers like Downys or Hairys, flickers are much larger, spend time on the ground, and have that distinctive wing flash. They're also the only local woodpecker with a spotted rather than striped or solid-colored breast.
